children.text: Just
15 minutes

from downtown Laoag, the La Paz Sand Dunes are coastal dunes formed by sand carried in by the sea and river and piled up by the wind. Racing up and down the sand ridges by 4x4 jeep, sliding down on a sandboard, and watching the sun set over the South China Sea are the highlights.

The La Paz Sand Dunes are coastal dunes spread across the village of La Paz, on the western coast of Laoag City near the mouth of the Laoag River. Sand carried down by the Laoag River and sand pushed up by the waves of the South China Sea have been blown and piled up by sea winds over a long time, creating a landscape of sand ridges tens of meters high and sunken valleys running one after another. Designated a national geological monument by the Philippine government, the site offers a "desert landscape" that is rarely seen on a tropical island nation.
Ilocos Norte's coastal dunes stretch along the shore from La Paz in Laoag south to Suba in Paoay. Both run 4x4 jeep tours: La Paz is the most accessible, just
15 minutes

from downtown Laoag by tricycle, while Suba pairs well with a visit to Paoay Church. Thanks to their stark, exotic look, these dunes have been used as a filming location many times, in both Philippine and foreign movies.

The star attraction here is unquestionably the 4x4 jeep tour. Modified jeeps race up the sand ridges at full speed and then plunge down steep slopes, a thrill as exciting as a roller coaster that keeps everyone screaming and laughing. The tour also includes stopping midway on a ridge for photos and sandboarding down a steep slope.
It suits adventurous groups of friends, families with children (elementary-school age or older recommended), and photographers alike. Since
1–2 hours
is enough, it's common to combine it with sightseeing in downtown Laoag or a visit to Paoay Church for a full-day itinerary.
On
November 26, 1993

, the Philippines' National Committee on Geological Sciences (NCGS) listed this dune area as a national geological monument under the name "Ilocos Norte Sand Dunes." More broadly, the dunes run along the coast from Currimao in the south, past Paoay and Laoag, to part of Pasuquin in the north, and their shape keeps changing with the strength and direction of the wind blowing in from the West Philippine Sea. The dunes are also famous as a filming location: in
, the crew of "Himala," starring Nora Aunor, searched for the driest land in the Philippines and shot around Paoay, and in Oliver Stone's "Born on the Fourth of July" (
), Ilocos Norte stood in for scenes set in Vietnam and Mexico.
The driver takes the jeep up and down the sand ridges at high speed, passing through steep drop sections several times. The basic route is about
20–30 minutes
(about
7 km
), and with photo stops and sandboarding it takes around
1 hour
; gripping the handles at the back seat tightly is a must.

Partway through the tour, you ride a board down a steep slope. If standing is too hard, lying face-down on the board or sitting and sledding down is plenty of fun too. Climbing back up through the sand is more of a workout than you'd expect.
Jump photos against the endless sand ridges and blue sky are the classic shot here. The drivers know all the photography tricks, so just ask and they'll take one for you.
Some operators also rent out ATVs (four-wheeled motorbikes). You can drive one yourself along a designated course, great for anyone who wants to try driving it.
From the western edge of the dunes, you can watch the sun set over the South China Sea. Start your tour after
and you can catch the sunset at the last stop.

The "Sinking Bell Tower," built in the early 17th century and now tilted from ground subsidence, along with St. William's Cathedral and the Ilocos Norte Museum, are all clustered in the city center, making them easy to visit before or after the dunes.

At the southern end of the dunes, in front of La Paz village, the Laoag River (Padsan River) flows into the sea. You can see the river meeting the sea and the fishermen's bangka boats, so it makes a quiet stroll with a different atmosphere from the dunes.
About
10 km
south of La Paz in a straight line, or about
30 minutes
by car, the dunes on the Suba side in Paoay also have 4x4, sandboarding, and ATV operators. A 4x4 costs about
per vehicle (up to 5 people), and an ATV about
for 2 people for 30 minutes. A monument commemorating the film "Himala" is a popular photo spot, so it pairs well with a visit to Paoay Church.

Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO), about
1 hour 10 minutes
, with one-way fares of roughly
depending on the season. It's
15–20 minutes
from the airport to downtown Laoag by tricycle or taxi, and about
15 minutes
from downtown to the La Paz Sand Dunes.
Laoag Airport lies south of the dunes, across the mouth of the Padsan River, only about
5 km

away in a straight line. The Manila route is flown by PAL Express and Cebu Pacific only a few times a day, so peak-season tickets sell out early, and flight numbers and times change often, so check the airlines' announcements.
Laoag-bound buses such as Partas, Fariñas Trans, and Maria de Leon run daily from the Cubao and Sampaloc terminals in Manila. The trip takes about
9–11 hours
, and fares are about
depending on class. From Vigan it takes about
2 hours
by Laoag-bound bus.
From
September 28, 2026
, provincial bus fares went up, and the benchmark per km after the first 5 km is
for aircon buses,
for deluxe,
for super deluxe, and

for luxury. Fares may be higher than the old ones still shown on booking sites, so check with the bus company before departure. Partas mainly departs from Cubao and Pasay, and Fariñas and GV Florida from Sampaloc; there are some daytime trips, but most are night buses that leave in the evening and arrive in the morning.
A tricycle is the easiest way from downtown Laoag to the La Paz Sand Dunes. One-way costs about
, or you can negotiate a round trip with the driver waiting through your tour for about

. A round-trip arrangement is recommended, since it can be hard to find a tricycle back during tour hours. Some 4x4 operators offer packages that include hotel pickup in the city. If you use the Suba dunes on the Paoay side instead, take a Paoay-bound jeepney from Laoag and transfer to a tricycle.
From Manila, take NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX, switch to MacArthur Highway at Rosario in La Union, and continue north past Vigan. The distance is about
and the drive takes about
8–10 hours
. Heading west from downtown Laoag toward La Paz village for about
15 minutes

brings you to the departure point where the operators' booths are clustered. An ordinary passenger car easily gets stuck in the sand and can't go far into the dunes, so park in front of the booths and transfer to an operator's 4x4.
Vigan: about
2 hours
by Laoag-bound bus or van, with a one-way fare of about
. If you leave Vigan around noon, you can make that afternoon's sunset tour.
Baguio: Partas and Fariñas run several direct buses to Laoag a day. It takes about
6–7 hours
and costs about
one-way; check the fare when you buy your ticket, as it changed after the
September 2026
increase.
The best time for a dune tour is the dry season, from
November
to
April
. The sand is dry then, so jeeps climb the ridges well and sandboards slide well. In
December–February
, mornings and evenings are cool and the strong wind creates beautiful ripple patterns on the sand.
In
March–May
, the sand surface gets very hot at midday, making it hard to walk barefoot, and sunlight reflection is intense. During this period, be sure to schedule your tour late in the afternoon, ideally after
During the rainy season from
June–October
, tours can be suspended when it rains, or the sand can get too wet for good sandboarding. From
July–September
, typhoons are frequent, so build extra time into flight and bus schedules. On the other hand, on clear days right after rain, there's less dust and the sky is clean, making for great photos.
Laoag's climate normals (
) show monthly rainfall under 10 mm from
December–March
, about 22 mm in April, and then a jump to about 219 mm in May as the rainy season begins. August is the wettest month (about 594 mm). The average January low is
, so a windbreaker is useful in the early morning, and the average high in April–May is
. During Holy Week (the week before Easter) and the year-end holidays, domestic travelers crowd in and 4x4 tours are busy at the afternoon sunset slot, and during the Pamulinawen Festival (
February 1–10
), held around the feast day of Laoag's patron saint, parades and performances fill the city.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There is almost no lodging around the dunes, so staying in downtown Laoag is the norm. The city center has many mid-range hotels and budget pensions priced around

per night. If you want a resort, Fort Ilocandia is a large property beside the dunes south of the city, with a pool and spacious grounds that suit family trips, and it also runs its own dune tour packages.

Laoag is the heartland of Ilocano cuisine. Be sure to try bagnet (pork belly fried twice for a crispy outside and moist inside), pinakbet (vegetables seasoned with bagoong), garlicky Laoag longganisa, and Batac empanada made from rice-flour dough. The empanada stalls around town are busiest in the evening, and dipping the empanada in spicy vinegar is the local way to eat it. For something sweet, try traditional rice cakes like tinubong, made by cooking glutinous rice and coconut milk in a bamboo tube.

Among the city's long-loved restaurants is La Preciosa, famous for Ilocano home cooking and thick carrot cake. Saramsam Ylocano on Rizal Street is decorated like an old Spanish-style mansion and is known for dishes that give Ilocos ingredients an Italian treatment, such as pinakbet pizza and longganisa pizza. For a cheap meal, look for the carinderias (local rice eateries) in the city, where you pick out bagnet and pinakbet. Good souvenirs are Ilocos vinegar, chichacorn (a corn snack), and basi, a sugarcane wine.
The best time to start the tour is
. The sand begins to cool by then, and you can catch the sunset at the end.
A jeep holds 4–5 people, so if your group is small you can also share a jeep with other travelers on site and split the cost.
Sand gets into every corner of your clothes and bag. Put your phone in a waterproof pouch or zip-lock bag, and don't change camera lenses while on the sand.
Sunglasses are a must, protecting your eyes from glare and blowing sand.
Closed shoes are better than sandals, though for sandboarding, bare feet are actually more comfortable — just avoid the hot midday sand.
Most places accept cash only. Withdraw money in advance from an ATM in downtown Laoag.
The back seats of the jeep are the most thrilling, while the front seat is relatively comfortable. If you get motion sick easily, ask for a front seat.
Climbing back up the sandy slope after sandboarding is tiring. Bring plenty of water.

You can sign up for a 4x4 tour directly at an operator's booth on site, or buy a package that includes hotel pickup in advance on booking sites such as Klook. The afternoon sunset slot is crowded on peak-season weekends, long weekends, and Holy Week, so it is safer to book the day before.
Operators generally take tours from around
until around
, when the sun sets. Hours differ by operator, so if you want an early-morning tour, contact them the day before.

The 4x4 tour has many steep drop sections and is not recommended for pregnant women or people with back, neck, or heart conditions. Young children should always be held by a guardian, or check the operator's age policy.
Only use officially licensed operators, and check the safety handles and seat condition before setting off.
At midday in
March–May
, the sand surface is very hot and heatstroke risk is high. Bring a hat, sunscreen, and water, and avoid touring around noon.
The interior of the dunes looks similar everywhere, so it's easy to get lost. Don't wander deep in on your own — stay with the driver.
The dune vegetation holds the sand in place and protects the landscape. Don't trample the grass or leave litter.
The Balikatan joint exercises of the Philippine and US militaries are held every year in April–May, and the La Paz dunes were used as a coastal-defense live-fire range in early May of
and
. During the exercises, a training camp is set up on the dunes and a no-sail zone is designated offshore, so if you go in spring, first check with the operator whether tours are running.
Just before the jeep crests a ridge, lean back and hold the handle with both hands. Standing up in excitement is the most dangerous moment.
